name: Supplier security questions
source: Grouped by the six functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, a work of the United States government and in the public domain. The wording of every question here is our own, written to be read easily.
answer_type: yes / no / partial, plus a note of up to 500 characters

full.label: Full
full.blurb: All forty questions. About half an hour.

questions.question: Is there one named job in your company that owns security decisions?
questions.why: A customer wants to know there is somebody whose job this is, not everybody and nobody.

questions.question: Do you have written security rules that your staff have to follow?
questions.why: Rules written down can be checked and taught. Rules in someone's head cannot.

questions.question: Do you look at those rules again at least once a year and change what is out of date?
questions.why: A customer wants to know the rules keep up with how you actually work.

questions.question: Do you check the security of the companies you buy software and services from?
questions.why: Your suppliers become your customer's suppliers. The risk travels down the chain.

questions.question: Do your contracts with those companies say what they must do if they have a break-in?
questions.why: A customer wants to know the duty to speak up is written down, not just hoped for.

questions.question: Do you keep a list of the laws and industry rules your business has to meet?
questions.why: It shows you know which rules apply to the work you do for this customer.

questions.question: Does a senior person see a written security update at least every three months?
questions.why: A customer wants to know problems reach the people who can pay to fix them.

questions.question: Do you keep an up-to-date list of the computers and servers your business uses?
questions.why: You cannot protect a machine you have forgotten you own.

questions.question: Do you keep a list of the software and online services your staff use for work?
questions.why: A customer wants to know their data is not sitting in a tool nobody signed off.

questions.question: Do you know which countries your customers' data is stored in?
questions.why: Where data sits changes which laws cover it, and some customers cannot use every country.

questions.question: Do you have a written list of the things most likely to go wrong and how bad each would be?
questions.why: It shows you have thought about failure before it happens, not after.

questions.question: Do you know which of your suppliers can reach your systems or your customers' data?
questions.why: A customer wants to know how many other companies can touch their information.

questions.question: Do you label data so staff can tell what is sensitive and what is not?
questions.why: Staff handle data carefully only when they can tell which data matters.

questions.question: Do you check at least once a year that these lists are still right?
questions.why: A list from three years ago tells a customer very little.

questions.question: Does every member of staff have their own login, never one shared between people?
questions.why: With a shared login nobody can tell afterwards who did what.

questions.question: Do staff need a second step to log in, such as a code on their phone?
questions.why: It is the single biggest thing that stops a stolen password turning into a break-in.

questions.question: Do you take away a person's access on the day they leave?
questions.why: Old logins that still work are one of the most common ways in.

questions.question: Do you give staff only the access they need for their own job?
questions.why: If one account is taken over, less access means less damage.

questions.question: Is customer data scrambled while it is stored, so a stolen disk is useless?
questions.why: A customer wants to know a lost laptop or drive does not hand over their records.

questions.question: Is data scrambled while it travels across the internet?
questions.why: It stops somebody in the middle reading the traffic.

questions.question: Do you put security updates on your computers and servers within 30 days?
questions.why: Most break-ins use a hole that was fixed months earlier.

questions.question: Do staff get security training at least once a year?
questions.why: Most attacks start with a person being tricked, not a machine being broken.

questions.question: Do you take backups and keep a copy where an attacker cannot reach it?
questions.why: If ransomware reaches your backups too, there is nothing to go back to.

questions.question: Do you control what staff can install on work computers?
questions.why: A customer wants to know their data is not next to software nobody checked.

questions.question: Do you keep records of who signed in and what they changed?
questions.why: Without records, nobody can work out afterwards what happened.

questions.question: Does something watch those records and raise an alarm when they look wrong?
questions.why: Records nobody reads do not catch anything while it is happening.

questions.question: Do staff laptops run protection that spots harmful software?
questions.why: A laptop is usually the first machine an attacker gets onto.

questions.question: Would you notice if a large amount of data left your systems at once?
questions.why: This is the question that decides whether a theft is caught in hours or in months.

questions.question: Do you scan your systems for known weak spots at least every three months?
questions.why: New holes are published every week, and old ones do not close themselves.

questions.question: Is somebody watching for alarms outside normal office hours?
questions.why: Attacks are timed for evenings, weekends and holidays on purpose.

questions.question: Do you have a written plan for what to do after a break-in?
questions.why: Nobody invents a good plan in the first hour of a real one.

questions.question: Have you practised that plan in the last twelve months?
questions.why: A plan that has never been tried usually has a hole in it.

questions.question: Would you tell affected customers, and within how long?
questions.why: A customer needs to know when they would hear, so they can plan their own response.

questions.question: Do you keep enough evidence afterwards for the cause to be worked out?
questions.why: If the evidence is wiped while tidying up, the same thing can happen again.

questions.question: Is there a published way for an outsider to report a security problem to you?
questions.why: Somebody who spots a hole should be able to tell you before they tell anybody else.

questions.question: Do you have a written plan for getting the service running again after a serious outage?
questions.why: A customer's own business stops when yours does.

questions.question: Do you know how long it would take to get back to normal, and have you written that number down?
questions.why: A customer needs a number they can plan around, not a promise.

questions.question: Have you restored real data from a backup in the last twelve months?
questions.why: Plenty of backups only fail on the day somebody first tries to use one.

questions.question: Do you tell customers what happened once the problem is fixed?
questions.why: A customer has to explain the outage to their own customers.

questions.question: After an incident, do you write down what you learned and change your rules?
questions.why: It is the difference between one bad week and the same bad week every year.
